common_name: Cherokee Pecan (Historic USDA Brownwood, Texas Release)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring while dormant. Pair with a cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable nut set. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Cherokee was one of a group of pecan cultivars named for Native American nations released from the USDA pecan field station at Brownwood, Texas, alongside Cheyenne, Choctaw, Mohawk, Shawnee, Sioux, and Wichita. It produces a medium-sized, well-filled nut on a vigorous tree and was valued for its productivity in Texas and Gulf South plantings during the mid-20th century. Like most older pecan releases from this program, it has only moderate scab resistance compared to newer USDA-ARS and university introductions, so it performs best with a fungicide program in humid areas or as a lower-spray option in drier western pecan regions. Site it in full sun with excellent drainage and plenty of room for its mature canopy.

common_name: Mohawk Pecan (Historic USDA Brownwood, Texas Release)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring while dormant. Pair with a cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable nut set. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Mohawk is another of the USDA Brownwood, Texas pecan station's Native American-nation-named releases, part of the same breeding effort that produced Cherokee, Cheyenne, Choctaw, Shawnee, Sioux, and Wichita. It bears a large, attractive nut with good kernel quality and was widely planted in Texas and the greater Southwest in the decades after its release. Scab susceptibility is a limitation in humid, high-rainfall climates, so it is best suited to drier western pecan-growing regions or home orchards willing to spray for disease. Give it full sun, deep well-drained soil, and ample spacing to reach its large mature size.

common_name: Comanche Pecan (Historic USDA Brownwood, Texas Release)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring while dormant. Pair with a cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable nut set. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Comanche rounds out the series of Native American-nation-named pecans released from the USDA's Brownwood, Texas field station, alongside Cherokee, Cheyenne, Choctaw, Mohawk, Shawnee, Sioux, and Wichita. It is known for precocious, early and heavy bearing of a good-quality nut, which made it popular with growers wanting quick production from young trees. As with its sibling releases from the same era, scab resistance is only moderate, so it is a better fit for drier western pecan regions or orchards maintaining a regular fungicide schedule. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and generous spacing.

common_name: Van Deman Pecan (Historic 1880s San Saba, Texas Native Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring while dormant. Pair with a cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable nut set. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Van Deman is one of the earliest named pecan cultivars to come out of the pioneering San Saba, Texas orchards of E.E. Risien in the late 1800s, honoring USDA pomologist H.E. Van Deman, who championed pecan grafting in that era. It is a native-type selection with a thinner shell and better kernel fill than typical seedling pecans of its day, though it has long since been surpassed in productivity and disease resistance by modern releases. It remains of interest mainly for heritage orchards and pecan breeding history, and performs best in the hot, relatively dry climate of its native west-central Texas range. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil.

common_name: Centennial Pecan (First Named Pecan Cultivar, Historic Louisiana Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring while dormant. Pair with a cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable nut set. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Centennial holds a unique place in pecan history as the first pecan tree ever propagated and sold under a cultivar name, traced to a seedling tree on the Oak Alley plantation in Louisiana grafted by an enslaved gardener remembered as Antoine around 1846-47 and later exhibited at the 1876 Centennial Exposition, where it earned its name. Its nuts are thin-shelled and well filled for a native-type Gulf South pecan of its era, though the tree is a lighter and less consistent bearer than modern scab-resistant cultivars. It is grown today mainly in historic orchards, botanical collections, and by growers interested in pecan breeding heritage. Plant in full sun in the humid Gulf South climate it originated in, with good drainage.

common_name: Delmas Pecan (Historic Early 1900s Mississippi Large-Nut Pecan)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring while dormant. Pair with a cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable nut set. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: Delmas is a historic Mississippi pecan cultivar from the early 1900s, prized in its day for a very large nut size and strong, productive growth along the Gulf Coast. It was widely planted in Mississippi and Louisiana dooryard and small commercial orchards before the arrival of modern scab-resistant releases, and it remains notably susceptible to pecan scab in humid years, limiting its use to low-spray heritage plantings or drier sites. Its large nuts and vigorous habit still make it a tree of interest for growers restoring historic Gulf Coast pecan orchards. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil.

common_name: Tombul Hazelnut (Classic Round Turkish Giresun Hazelnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-incompatible, so plant with a distinct pollenizer cultivar for a reliable crop.

directions: Tombul, meaning round or plump in Turkish, is the benchmark cultivar of the Giresun region on Turkey's Black Sea coast, long considered among the finest hazelnuts in the world for its round shape, thin shell, and rich, easily-peeled kernel. It is moderately vigorous and productive but has little resistance to Eastern Filbert Blight, so it is best suited to regions where the disease is not established or to growers prepared to manage it closely. The tree benefits from a humid, maritime-influenced climate similar to its native coastal growing region and responds well to regular pruning to maintain an open, multi-stemmed habit. Harvest in late summer to early fall once husks brown and nuts loosen.

common_name: Du Chilly Hazelnut (Historic Long-Nutted Oregon Cracking Filbert)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-incompatible, so plant with a distinct pollenizer cultivar for a reliable crop.

directions: Du Chilly is a historic European hazelnut cultivar long grown in Oregon's Willamette Valley for its distinctively long, cylindrical nut, once prized for the whole-in-shell novelty and cracking trade rather than for kernel percentage alone. It is highly susceptible to Eastern Filbert Blight and has largely been removed from commercial orchards in favor of EFB-resistant releases, so it is grown today mostly by home growers and heritage orchardists. The tree is moderately vigorous with an upright habit, and performs best in the cool, moist Pacific Northwest climate it was historically grown in. Harvest in early fall as husks brown and nuts loosen from their husks.
sources: Oregon State University Department of Horticulture

common_name: Fertile de Coutard Hazelnut (Historic French Noisette du Perigord Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-incompatible, so plant with a distinct pollenizer cultivar for a reliable crop.

directions: Fertile de Coutard is a long-cultivated French hazelnut variety and one of the traditional cultivars behind the Noisette du Perigord designation in southwestern France, valued for consistent fruitfulness and good-flavored, medium-sized kernels. It is a reliable, moderately vigorous producer in cool to mild temperate climates but, like most old European cultivars, carries no resistance to Eastern Filbert Blight, making it best suited to regions where the disease pressure is low. The tree suckers readily in the classic hazelnut habit and benefits from periodic removal of old wood to keep production concentrated on younger stems. Harvest in early to mid fall as husks brown and nuts drop freely.

common_name: Casina Hazelnut (Italian Piedmont Nocciola Pollenizer Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-incompatible, so plant with a distinct pollenizer cultivar such as San Giovanni or Tonda Gentile delle Langhe for a reliable crop.

directions: Casina is a traditional Italian hazelnut cultivar grown in the Piedmont region as one of the accessory varieties permitted alongside Tonda Gentile delle Langhe in the Nocciola Piemonte protected geographical indication, where it serves mainly as an effective pollenizer with good bloom overlap. Its own nuts are smaller and less commercially prized than Tonda Gentile but are still usable for roasting and processing. The tree is vigorous and productive, adapted to the hilly, well-drained growing areas of northwestern Italy's hazelnut belt. Harvest in late summer to early fall as husks brown and nuts loosen.

common_name: San Giovanni Hazelnut (Italian Piedmont Nocciola Pollenizer Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-incompatible, so plant with a distinct pollenizer cultivar such as Casina or Tonda Gentile delle Langhe for a reliable crop.

directions: San Giovanni is another traditional Piedmont hazelnut cultivar recognized, alongside Casina, as an accessory variety within Italy's Nocciola Piemonte protected geographical indication, grown chiefly to extend bloom overlap and improve pollination of the dominant Tonda Gentile delle Langhe. It produces a moderately sized nut of lesser commercial value than the main cultivar but contributes to orchard reliability in off years. The tree is well adapted to the hilly terrain and moderate climate of the Langhe and surrounding hazelnut-growing districts of northwestern Italy. Harvest in late summer to early fall as husks brown and nuts loosen.
